$comment: Riftlight authored opening draft. Development preview only; see ../README.md. Production campaign id will be riftlight. No bonus XP: preserve the design bible campaign budget.
title: The Island Due Back

goal.text: Help the keepers meet the island that is due back.

steps.label: Spot the island in the clouds

voiceGuide.tone: Warm, funny, curious, with real consequences. Describe actions and sensory details directly. Short dialogue. Never use "the kind of thing that", "the sort of thing that", or "it was X, the type of thing that makes you Y" comparisons. Let a character act instead of explaining how the reader should feel.
voiceGuide.vocabulary: Read aloud to an eight-year-old. Concrete words, short sentences, distinct voices.

npcVoices.Pip Thistledown: Eager manticore scout. Asks before guessing, repeats signals, and credits another observer.
npcVoices.Kitsune keeper: Practical, welcoming navigator. Uses songs alongside observations; never knows an unseen cause.

arrival.narration: Beyond the whales' turning place, a kitsune keeper stands beside a lookout bell. Pip Thistledown, the manticore scout, holds the bell rope clear of his tail. A low, flat island is appearing beneath the cloud. On the grass lie a folded landing board, signal cloths and a wooden box of song slips. "That one is due back," the keeper says. "We have sung for its return since before I was born. I expected more time to get the board out." Pip takes a breath. "What needs doing first?"

variants.text: The scattered cloud whales have not returned to the lookout. The keeper has lost the circling song she usually listens for before an island comes in. "We will need sightings from the ground," she says. Nobody claims to know where the whales went.

The cloud whales you guided clear are singing beyond the open lane. The keeper hears a turning note and points beneath the cloud. "They have seen something low. We should look there first." Their song offers a place to look, not a promise about where the island will stop.

return_song.narration: The keeper opens the box of song slips. Each slip carries a line and the marks for its tune; together they describe the island expected after a long circuit. The oldest line says "a flat brow, a notch, a stone with an empty eye." Pip looks from the slips to the shape beneath the cloud. The keeper offers to sing the line again while you look, or let you arrange the slips on the ground. "A song can tell us what to look for. It cannot make this the right island." How will you test the welcome?

choices.label: Sing the signs while Pip points them out
Lay out the signs and leave unknown ones blank

return_song_1.narration: You take one sign at a time. Pip finds a low brow, then the notch. A round hole through a standing stone is still hidden by mist. You leave that part of the song unanswered. The keeper smiles at the silence. "We can wait for a thing we have not seen."

return_song_2.narration: You set the slips in order and put a pebble beside the two shapes you can see. The empty-eye stone stays unmarked. Pip tries to add a pebble for it, catches himself and puts the pebble back in his pocket. "Two signs. One question," he says.

sightings.narration: A notch on the approaching island slides past a distant cloud break. The keeper pushes two short sighting sticks into firm grass, well away from the edge. She needs to know which side of the lookout the island will pass before anyone lays out the landing board. The nearest cloud is moving too; a single glance could make the island seem to turn. You can compare the notch from both sticks or watch its movement against a fixed corner of the lookout roof. Which view will you trust enough to test?

choices.label: Compare the notch from two fixed viewpoints
Time the notch against the lookout roof
Use the guided whales' turning note

sightings_1.narration: You and Pip take the two sticks. Each calls only when the notch lines up, while the keeper counts the beats between calls. Nobody walks backward toward the edge. You repeat the sighting rather than change a report to make both agree.

sightings_1_check.prompt: Compare the notch from two fixed viewpoints. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

sightings_1_done.narration: Your two calls make a clear sequence: the island will pass below the left side of the lookout. The keeper moves the loose board to that side. A second sighting agrees. There is still work before a crossing, but the waiting place is no longer a guess.

sightings_1_changed.narration: A cloud hides the notch before your second call. You leave the missing sighting blank. The keeper keeps the board folded until the island comes fully into view; then she moves it to the left. Waiting costs preparation time, not anyone's footing.

sightings_2.narration: Pip holds a string upright beside the roof corner. You watch from the marked grass and call when the notch passes it. The keeper listens to a second count before moving any equipment. The roof gives a fixed edge even when the clouds change shape.

sightings_2_check.prompt: Time the notch against the lookout roof. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

sightings_2_done.narration: Two careful counts put the island below the left side of the lookout. The keeper shifts the folded board there while the ground between you is clear. Pip ties a little knot in his string for the count; the knot is a note, not a mooring line.

sightings_2_changed.narration: Your first count follows the cloud instead of the notch. Pip catches the mismatch and lowers the string. You wait for the island to clear the mist, then the keeper moves the board to the left. Nobody turns an uncertain count into permission to cross.

priority.narration: A gust lifts the corner of the song box and sets it rattling. At the same time, a messenger's loose shoulder bag slides down the grassy slope toward a low fence. A keeper has hold of the messenger; nobody is falling. The bag carries sealed letters for moving addresses. The open lookout has the song slips and the cloth you will need for signals. Two keepers can cover whichever job you leave them, but they cannot finish both before the next gust. Your party can recover the letters or make the signal station ready. Which work do you take?

choices.label: Recover the messenger bag before the next gust
Secure the song slips and signal station

priority_1.narration: You tell the keeper to cover the song box. Pip watches the bag lodge against a fence post and points out a path across the slope. The messenger asks you to leave the letters sealed. You agree. Saving a letter does not make its contents yours to read.

priority_2.narration: You ask the messenger to help the other keeper reach the bag. Your party stays at the lookout. Pip puts both paws on the song box while the keeper brings a cover and spare cloth ties. She needs the slips dry and the signals loose enough to lift.

letters.narration: The messenger bag hangs against the inside of the low fence. Its strap catches whenever the gust pulls it outward. From the firm path above, you can reach it with a loop on a long pole; or you can pass a line along the fence and draw it sideways to a gate. The keeper holds the slope clear. Nobody needs to climb beyond the fence or fly into the wind. The messenger points to a stout seam on the bag. "That part can take a pull. The flap cannot." Which way will you bring it in?

choices.label: Lift the strap with a looped pole
Draw the bag sideways along the fence
Have a duskrunner secure the bag strap

letters_1.narration: You open the loop wider than the strap and let the gust settle before lowering it. Pip keeps the pole from swinging across anyone's face. The messenger calls when the stout seam faces the path. Your party can take turns without putting more weight on the fence.

letters_1_check.prompt: Lift the strap with a looped pole. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

letters_1_done.narration: The loop catches the strap and you lift the bag onto the path. The sealed letters are dry. Their owner hugs the bag, then checks the seal on each packet. She can leave with the first clear signal instead of spending the afternoon making replacements.

letters_1_changed.narration: The loop slips off as the gust changes. You draw the pole back. A keeper reaches the gate below and retrieves the bag after the wind settles, but water has entered one corner. The messenger keeps the sealed packets to dry; she cannot promise an immediate delivery.

letters_2.narration: You pass the line through the gate rather than over the outer edge. Pip guides it under a low rail. The messenger shows you how to support the bag from beneath so the paper inside does not take the strain. Your party pulls only on her count.

letters_2_check.prompt: Draw the bag sideways along the fence. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

letters_2_done.narration: The bag travels along the inside of the fence and comes through the gate. Every sealed letter is dry. The messenger checks them without opening them and offers to carry an authorized warning as soon as your signal is ready. Your rescue has saved her departure time.

letters_2_changed.narration: The line catches on the fence post. You stop instead of pulling the bag apart. The keeper below works it free later; one corner has soaked through. The messenger must dry the sealed packets before leaving, so a fast warning will need the lookout flags.

station.narration: The song slips flutter inside their open box. Beside it stands a low signal frame with two cloths tied at the bottom; one tie has worked loose. The keeper can hold the cover while you secure the frame, or pin the cloth while you move the box under the lookout roof. The frame carries warnings, not the weight of an island. It must turn freely enough for another keeper to read both cloths. Pip tests his grip and waits for your plan. Which part will you settle first?

choices.label: Brace the frame while the keeper fixes its ties
Move the box under cover and retie from shelter

station_1.narration: You stand on the landward side of the frame and steady its feet. The keeper replaces the loose tie without binding the turning arm. Pip holds the cover over the box. Your party calls a halt whenever a gust makes someone shift their stance.

station_1_check.prompt: Brace the frame while the keeper fixes its ties. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

station_1_done.narration: The frame stays level through the next gust. The keeper lifts both cloths and turns them toward the neighboring temple lookout; they fall freely when she lowers them. The song slips stay dry. You have a working station for a warning that must be seen quickly.

station_1_changed.narration: One foot slides in the wet grass. You lower the frame together and keep the box covered. The keeper will repair the footing before using it. Until then, signals must be carried by hand from the shelter; they will take an extra relay.

station_2.narration: You pass the box hand to hand beneath the lookout roof. Pip holds the cloth still while you copy the keeper's knot on the loose tie. You check that it releases as well as holds; a cloth trapped against its frame cannot carry a useful warning.

station_2_check.prompt: Move the box under cover and retie from shelter. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

station_2_done.narration: The box is dry under the roof and both cloths lift cleanly. The keeper checks your knot and turns the frame toward the neighboring temple lookout. Someone there raises a small answering cloth. The station is ready before the island has finished coming into view.

station_2_changed.narration: The wet tie tightens around the turning arm. You lower the cloth instead of tearing it free. The keeper covers the slips and starts loosening the knot. Hand-carried signals remain possible, but the station needs repair before anyone can rely on it.

signal_plan.narration: The keeper lays a white cloth and a striped cloth on the grass. White means "watch this approach"; striped means "stop and wait." Pip volunteers to stand at the far end of the marked ground, where he can see the island and your party. He can repeat each signal so you know it reached him, or watch continuously while the keeper calls the changes. The keeper makes both signs slowly before asking you to use them. Neither sign orders the island around. They tell people when to move. Which arrangement will you practice?

choices.label: Have Pip repeat each sign before anyone moves
Keep Pip watching the island and use the keeper's call

signal_plan_1.narration: Pip lifts the same cloth only after he sees yours. You wait for his answer, then take one step along the grass. The keeper changes to striped. Everyone stops. Repeating the sign uses a little time now, but it catches a cloth hidden by a shoulder before a crossing depends on it.

signal_plan_2.narration: Pip keeps both eyes on the island while the keeper calls each change from beside you. You practice a step, a halt and a return. You have one lookout devoted to movement, though anyone who misses a call must stop and ask again. The keeper refuses to count silence as agreement.

bearings.narration: The returning island clears the cloud with a flat shelf facing the lookout. A round hole through its standing stone gives the song its third sign: the empty eye. Between the islands, strips of mist reveal the gap widening and narrowing. The keeper has a short landing board with side ropes, long enough only when the shelves draw close. She will lay it down after two matching observations, and lift it if they disagree. Do you measure the gap with the board's painted marks or call the two shelves' closest points in rhythm?

choices.label: Compare the gap with the board's painted marks
Call the shelves' closest points together

bearings_1.narration: You keep the board on your own grass and use its painted lengths as a sighting scale. Pip signals from the far mark on the lookout ground. The keeper repeats your measure aloud before making the next one. Nobody tests the distance by stepping into it.

bearings_1_check.prompt: Compare the gap with the board's painted marks. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

bearings_1_done.narration: Two measures agree on a narrow, steady gap. The keeper points to the painted limit that makes the board usable. Pip records where the shelves line up so the return can be checked too. You have verified a crossing window rather than guessed from one lucky glance.

bearings_1_changed.narration: Your two measures disagree. The keeper keeps the board back while the island slides a little farther past. She takes the next pair herself and finds a shorter window. You can still cross with her watching every step, but your own estimate is not marked as verified.

bearings_2.narration: Pip calls from his lookout mark while you watch the near shelf. The keeper keeps a beat with one finger on the board. You call only when the two edges hold their closest alignment for a full beat. A fast shout does not lengthen the board.

bearings_2_check.prompt: Call the shelves' closest points together. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

bearings_2_done.narration: Your calls agree for two full beats. The keeper marks the board's safe limit and Pip notes the position for the return. The crossing window is small but checked by your observers. You can explain exactly which alignment you used without promising that it will last.

bearings_2_changed.narration: A gust covers one call. You stop the count instead of pretending everyone heard. The keeper takes a second set of observations and offers a shorter, supervised window. Your party can cross safely on her signals, but your own timing stays an unfinished test.

bearings_relay.narration: Pip repeats your cloth before the next measure. A gust hides your first sign; because you wait for his answer, nobody mistakes it for permission. The keeper gives you the board scale and asks for the same two observations. Your preparation makes the communication clearer, while the gap still needs checking.

bearings_relay_check.prompt: Compare the gap with the board's painted marks. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

landing.narration: The keeper lays the landing board across the close shelves. Side ropes stand at hand height. A second keeper crosses first to secure the far side. Nobody is asked to hold either island still. Pip checks that the striped stop cloth is visible from both ends. Your party will cross one at a time with the keepers watching the changing gap. A gust presses the empty board sideways. You can steady its near foot while the keeper secures it, or check the side ropes and guide the first steps. Which job do you take? The shelves are traveling alongside one another for now. The keepers will watch the gap throughout the visit and call you back before lifting the board.

choices.label: Steady the board while its foot is secured
Check the side ropes and guide careful steps
Have a thornguard brace the landing board

variants.text: Pip has your checked alignment ready for the return. He can repeat it while the keeper watches for a change.
The keeper assigns a second lookout to the return gap because your own estimate was unfinished. Pip repeats her calls rather than presenting them as your measurement.

landing_1.narration: You work from the near grass. The keeper secures the board's foot to its own small landing stake; she leaves room to lift it free if the islands separate. Pip waits for the white cloth before calling anyone forward. The stake carries the board, not the drifting land.

landing_1_check.prompt: Steady the board while its foot is secured. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

landing_1_done.narration: The board stays square while the keeper secures its foot. Your party crosses in order and waits behind the far rope. Pip brings up the end without jumping. The second keeper checks the alignment again before allowing the lookout helpers to cross after you.

landing_1_changed.narration: The gust shifts the board before its foot is secure. Everyone steps onto grass. You lift the board together. Before laying it again, your party must reduce the load or change how it carries the kit.

landing_2.narration: You follow the side ropes from knot to knot while still on the near shelf. The keeper checks the far ends. Pip watches the stop cloth, and your party practices a halt before the first person steps onto the board. Wings and tails get room without changing the walking route.

landing_2_check.prompt: Check the side ropes and guide careful steps. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

landing_2_done.narration: The side ropes hold their clear line and each traveler can see the next handhold. The keeper keeps the board square while your party crosses. Pip waits until the last person is on grass before he moves. The helpers follow only after a fresh check of the gap.

landing_2_changed.narration: A side rope sags during the practice halt. You return to grass and lower the board. The keeper replaces the rope while your party decides what to carry on the next close alignment.

stone_care.narration: On the returning island, the standing stone has a round hole and a broad carved face. The keeper calls it an old mooring stone: ropes once ran through the eye, but nobody proposes tying today's islands together with it. Dry grass lies over its foot. Shallow grooves cross the face in branching lines, with three raised shapes between them. Pip reaches for a loose stalk, then waits. The keeper has a soft brush and a blank sheet. "We came to welcome it. We can look without taking it apart." What do you protect before reading?

choices.label: Keep people off the carved face and mark a viewing place
Make a clean place for tools and loose grass

stone_care_1.narration: You lay the blank sheet on grass and mark where people may stand. Pip bends a tall stalk to make the line visible, leaving its root in place. The keeper moves a loose carrying sack away from the grooves. Nothing rests on the stone while you read.

stone_care_2.narration: You spread the blank sheet on firm grass for the brush and the loose stalks. Pip checks each stalk before setting it down so no tool gets buried in the pile. The keeper keeps everyone on one side of the stone while its shallow marks come into view.

carving.narration: The shallow grooves are hard to separate from the grass shadows. The keeper offers the soft brush for loose dust, or the blank sheet to hold beside the stone as a shade. Neither method scratches a line or makes a rubbing across a worn surface. Two grooves almost meet beneath the eye; a crack runs past them at another angle. If you copy the crack as a road, the rest of the drawing will tell a different story. How will you make a record that leaves uncertain marks visibly uncertain?

choices.label: Brush loose dust and copy only clear grooves
Shade the face and copy it from the side

carving_1.narration: You move the brush across a small patch while the keeper watches for flaking stone. Pip holds the drawing upright beside the face. You mark a gap wherever the brush cannot safely clear the groove. The keeper asks you to include that gap in the copy rather than improve the old carving.

carving_1_check.prompt: Brush loose dust and copy only clear grooves. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

carving_1_done.narration: Loose dust falls away from the joined grooves. Their carved edges are rounded alike; the sharp crack cuts across both. You can show where the two old lines meet without drawing the crack into them. Pip leaves a dotted patch where the stone is still worn.

carving_1_changed.narration: Dust hides the meeting point. You stop before the brush catches a loose edge. The keeper can show you the broad pattern, but the little join stays dotted on your drawing. A readable clue does not require every worn line to become a confident new one.

carving_2.narration: You and Pip hold the sheet beside the stone so it shades the glare without rubbing the surface. The keeper watches the old grooves from the side. You change the sheet's angle slowly, checking that a moving shadow does not become a copied mark.

carving_2_check.prompt: Shade the face and copy it from the side. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

carving_2_done.narration: In the even shade the two grooves meet cleanly beneath the eye. The crack stays sharp and separate. You copy both kinds of mark with different strokes. Pip points out the worn corner and you leave it dotted; the clearer join does not repair that missing piece.

carving_2_changed.narration: The sheet flickers in the gust. A shadow seems to join two lines, then moves away. You lower the sheet and copy the broad pattern with the keeper's help. The meeting point stays dotted so nobody later mistakes the shifting shadow for something carved.

orientation.narration: The keeper sets a present-day lookout sketch beside your copy. Three separate ridges show through the cloud below. The stone has three raised marks with grooves between them. Its rope groove gives the carved face a fixed top. Pip can hold the papers upright or call the visible ridges from the viewing mark. How will you compare without turning the copy to force a fit?

choices.label: Keep the old rope groove at the top of both copies
Have Pip name each visible ridge from the viewing mark

orientation_1.narration: You mark a small top arrow on the copy and Pip keeps it beside the stone. The keeper turns the lookout sketch to its own marked direction. A ridge that does not agree stays visible as a problem. Nobody folds the paper to bring the channels together.

orientation_2.narration: Pip stands at the mark and describes the left ridge, the notch and the broad back of the third. You point to each shape on the upright copy. The keeper checks from beside him. Cloud covers the lowest ground, so nobody claims to have seen what lies under it.

comparison.narration: Three raised marks appear on your copy beside the present lookout sketch. The sketch shows three separate ridges. Between the old marks, shallow grooves bend and meet; a worn patch interrupts one line. Are these the same places, and what does the space between them show? The keeper holds the papers still. Pip offers his grass measuring stalk. Choose a comparison before deciding what the old lines mean.

choices.label: Compare the order and spacing of the three ridges
Follow the channel past each fixed ridge
Use the clearly recorded carved join

variants.text: Your copy separates the carved join from the later crack. The keeper can ask another reader to inspect that distinction directly.
Your meeting point remains dotted. The keeper sets the present lookout sketch beside it, leaving that gap for your party to work around.

comparison_1.narration: You keep the top arrow fixed and measure the spaces with a grass stalk. Pip compares ratios rather than the size of the paper. The keeper asks you to point out a fourth shape if you think one exists. There are only three clear matches; you do not invent another.

comparison_1_check.prompt: Compare the order and spacing of the three ridges. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

comparison_1_done.narration: Your stalk marks fit the three ridge spaces without turning the paper. Now you follow the surface carved between them: it continues where the present sketch has gaps. "There is ground all the way across!" Pip says. Your comparison shows that the land was joined here. You keep the measurements beside the copy. The date and cause stay blank.

comparison_1_changed.narration: The worn middle mark will not give a clean measure. You stop with two distances that disagree. The keeper leaves both papers in your hands. Which different comparison could your party try?

comparison_2.narration: You follow one clear groove above the paper while Pip keeps the raised marks fixed. The keeper checks that you have not turned the copy. At the worn patch you stop; the next clear stretch must fit the same order before you connect anything.

comparison_2_check.prompt: Follow the channel past each fixed ridge. Choose who leads; everyone can help from the marked ground.

comparison_2_done.narration: Your finger follows the groove past all three fixed ridge marks. The carved surface continues between them; today's lookout sketch separates those same heights. Your tracing shows that the land was joined here. Pip puts a finger in each present-day gap, then lifts them to reveal the difference. You record the clear route and leave the worn patch dotted.

comparison_2_changed.narration: The dotted patch hides the middle turn. You cannot finish that tracing. Pip lowers his measuring stalk and the keeper waits. Your party can try a different comparison without pretending the missing turn is visible.

alternative.narration: Pip looks from the stone to the lookout sketch. "The land was joined here. But when?" Neither the stone nor the return song gives a date for that view. The keeper asks what you would need to test next. Challenge whether the marks describe land, or ask what could date the change.

choices.label: Could this be a pattern instead of a view?
What would let us date or explain this change?

alternative_1.narration: You ask the keeper to show where decoration ends and a claim about land begins. She points to the three matching ridges and the channel between them. That local fit gives you a reason to compare; it does not supply the missing age or explain why the islands move.

alternative_2.narration: The keeper asks for a dated account from the same place and another view to compare. Neither is present on the stone. Pip writes those needs beneath the drawing. The party leaves with a clear clue and a clear limit, rather than a date borrowed from the song of return.

record.narration: The keeper asks permission to keep a copy of your observations. She will leave the stone where it stands and take no chip, token or rubbing from it. Your sketch can travel with you whether or not she gets a second one. Pip holds the pencil over a blank credit line. A shared copy will let other lookout keepers challenge the match; a private account will stay in your party's hands. Either way, the keeper will use her own observations for public warnings. What may she copy from your work?

choices.label: Share the checked observations with their limits

variants.text: Your own comparison succeeded. If you share it, the keeper will credit the party's test and retain the measurements or ridge order that supports it.
Your first comparison was unfinished. The shared account can credit the follow-up your party made with help, while keeping the failed measure or missing turn visible.

record_1.narration: You let the keeper copy the observations and write who supplied each part. Pip keeps the blanks and dotted marks in both copies. No old maker's name or date is added. A later reader can question your work without being told that the party solved every line.

record_2.narration: You keep the sketch with your party. The keeper closes her copying sheet and thanks you for helping on the island. She retains her own observations and does not retell your private account as permission to publish it. Pip leaves the unused credit line blank.

departure.narration: The returning island continues past the lookout instead of stopping. Farther along its course, a temple island lifts a line of roofs above the cloud. The keeper checks the gap and prepares the landing board for the return; there is time for everyone to walk back under her signals. Pip points to the moving island's direction. "They should know it is coming." The keeper agrees. She can send a course warning now or use the first message for an invitation to inspect the old stone. Neither message needs your private sketch. Which goes first?

choices.label: Send the temple a course warning first
Invite another keeper to inspect the stone first

variants.text: The messenger's dry bag is ready. She offers to carry this authorized message on her next clear departure; saving her letters has preserved that option.
The signal frame you prepared is already answering the temple lookout. The keeper can send a short course warning without waiting for the hand relay.
Your batch-carrying plan keeps the messenger relay waiting for the return. Choose the first message now; it will leave after your party finishes bringing the kit back.

departure_1.narration: You ask for a warning with the island's observed direction and the places still hidden by cloud. The keeper leaves the unknown speed blank until her next sighting. Pip repeats the striped wait sign for travelers at the lookout. An invitation can follow after the temple has time to prepare.

departure_2.narration: You ask for a second reader to inspect the old face independently. The keeper sends that invitation with a note that the island is still moving. Her routine course report will follow on the next relay; your first message does not claim that the temple has already been warned.

return.narration: The keepers check the landing board again and guide your party back across while the shelves are still close. They lift the board after the last helper steps onto grass. You put the keeper's brush back in her kit; your sketch stays with your party. The returning island moves on without a rope trying to hold it. Pip watches the stone's empty eye vanish into cloud. Your party has seen an old local view in which land between three familiar ridges was joined. Its date and cause remain unknown. There is enough to compare with another discovery, and more work ahead along the island's course.

variants.text: The first message is the course warning. The keeper marks when it left and waits for an answer before claiming the temple has received it.
The first message asks for another reader. The keeper marks the course warning for the next relay; nobody claims your invitation has already prepared the temple.
The messenger sets off with her sealed letters dry. She carries only the message you authorized, not a copy of private notes.
The station cloths lift freely as the keeper sends the next sign. The song slips stay dry beneath the roof.
Pip asks your party to repeat the test it completed before he adds its result to his own notes.
Pip records the follow-up your party made with help. The first unfinished test remains marked beside the discovery.
The keeper stores the shared copy with its credit and limits. She makes no promise that it explains the rest of the realm.
Your private sketch stays with your party. The keeper files only her own observations.
Your party finishes the last batch of carrying before the waiting messenger relay can leave. The keeper sends your chosen first message now, later than a light-kit crossing would have allowed.

rest.narration: The lookout bell rings once as the next watcher takes the rope. Your party rests on the grass with the board safely stowed. The old mooring stone gives your party a clue about the land below. It is knowledge to compare, not a piece broken off the island. Beyond the cloud, the moving island is still heading toward the temple route. You may return to the whales' turning place or pause this development preview here.

landing_brace.narration: A thornguard uses brace from the near grass while the keeper secures the board foot. Pip watches the stop cloth. The qualified hero supplies support; whoever can best judge the load may lead. The board still has to be secured, and the islands remain free to drift.

landing_brace_check.prompt: Have a thornguard brace the landing board. The qualified hero helps; choose who leads the team check.

letters_runner.narration: A duskrunner threads the recovery loop through the strap from the firm path. Pip steadies the pole. The qualified hero supplies the quick hands while your best roller leads the lift. Nobody climbs beyond the fence, and the sealed letters stay closed.

letters_runner_check.prompt: Have a duskrunner secure the bag strap. The qualified hero helps; choose who leads the team check.

sightings_whales.narration: The whales beyond the clear lane turn together. The keeper listens to their low note while your party sights the notch from the marked ground. The song tells you where to look first; you still need to confirm the fixed view. You do not call or ride the whales.

sightings_whales_check.prompt: Confirm the sighting using the whales' turning note. Choose who compares the fixed views.

comparison_clear.narration: You point out the rounded carved join and the sharp crack that your copy kept separate. The keeper holds the present lookout sketch upright while Pip checks the three ridges. The clearer record removes one uncertainty, but the local match still needs testing.

comparison_clear_check.prompt: Use the clearly recorded carved join. The qualified hero helps; choose who leads the team check.

comparison_recovery.narration: Two clear marks remain on either side of the worn patch. Ask the keeper to hold a scale while you match their spacing, or ask Pip to point out the same two heights from the viewing mark while you trace around them. Both methods leave the worn part unanswered. Who will help your party test the clear parts?

choices.label: Measure two clear marks with the keeper
Trace the two clear heights with Pip

comparison_recover_scale.narration: You place the stalk across the two clear marks while the keeper holds the scale. They fit the two outer ridges. Your finger follows the carved surface between them: the land was joined here, where today's sketch has gaps. The keeper asks you to show Pip. You can, while leaving the worn middle mark dotted.

comparison_recover_view.narration: Pip points from the viewing mark while your party follows the two clear outer heights on the copy. The surface carved between them continues across today's gaps: the land was joined here. You show the keeper the difference you noticed. Your first tracing is still unfinished, and its missing bend stays dotted.

landing_recovery.narration: The keeper can lend a pocket brush and spare a sheet if you leave the bulky equipment here. Or your party can carry everything in small batches, helping with a longer hand relay before any messenger leaves. The keepers will check the board each time. Which cost do you accept?

choices.label: Carry the kit in batches; delay the message relay
Leave bulky gear and borrow the keeper's small kit

landing_batches.narration: You pass small loads along the grass, then cross on the keeper's checked alignment. Pip waits with each batch. The complete kit reaches the island, but the messenger relay must wait until everyone returns. You have chosen extra carrying work over borrowing tools. The keepers help carry too; even a prepared signal frame must wait for its sender.

landing_borrow.narration: You stack the bulky kit under the lookout roof. The keeper lends her pocket brush and gives you a folded sheet. You will return the brush before leaving. With hands free for the side ropes, your party crosses on the checked alignment. The message relay can keep its place.
